Gastroenterology · published research

Reflux laryngitis

Two rat experiments found fewer inflammatory cells and improved repair measures after different PBM protocols. No clinical study has tested whether these tissue findings improve reflux-related symptoms in people.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two rat experiments found fewer inflammatory cells and improved repair measures after different PBM protocols. No clinical study has tested whether these tissue findings improve reflux-related symptoms in people.

Summary of the Evidence

Two publications from one Brazilian research team tested PBM in rat models of reflux laryngitis induced by nasogastric intubation. They used different red and infrared protocols. The records describe two experiments, but do not establish whether the animals were entirely separate, so they should be treated as two related reports rather than independent replication by different teams. No human study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical trial has tested PBM for reflux laryngitis in people. The animal model examines short-term tissue inflammation and repair after a defined procedure. It does not measure hoarseness, throat discomfort, cough, swallowing, voice quality, or recurrence in patients.

Animal evidence

In the 2013 experiment, combined 780-nm near-infrared light and 660-nm red visible light reduced neutrophil infiltration, modulated mast-cell degranulation, and improved granulation tissue formation and collagen deposition in the injured larynx. These are favorable inflammatory and repair findings within the intubation-induced rat model (Marinho et al. 2013).

In the 2014 study, 780-nm near-infrared treatment reduced neutrophil influx and improved reparative collagenization after laryngitis was induced by a nasogastric tube. This provides a second report with a similar tissue direction, although it is from the same team and model family (Marinho et al. 2014).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No cell-culture or ex-vivo PBM study directly examining reflux laryngitis was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2013 protocol combined 780-nm near-infrared light at 17.5 J/cm² with 660-nm red visible light at 10 J/cm², applied for 30 seconds at three points over four sessions. The 2014 protocol used 780-nm near-infrared light at 105 J/cm² for 180 seconds at three points, also over four sessions. The different fluences and protocols have not been compared in a dose-finding trial. Neither animal delivery schedule establishes an effective dose for the human larynx.

Interpretation

Both experiments found less inflammatory-cell activity or improved tissue repair after PBM. The results are favorable for short-term histology in this induced rat model, but do not establish relief of human reflux-laryngitis symptoms or lasting laryngeal healing.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for reduced inflammation and improved tissue repair in induced rat laryngitis
Publications and records2 related articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two rat studies reported fewer inflammatory cells and better repair measures, but both came from the same research team and used a procedure-induced model. No human study has tested symptoms, voice, or endoscopic healing. Replication by another group, followed by a controlled patient study with symptom and laryngeal outcomes, would support a stronger rating.
